questions.q: What happens when you call a function defined with `async def`, without using `await`?
options: The function body runs immediately, just like a normal function
Python raises a SyntaxError
It returns a coroutine object — a paused task that hasn't actually run yet
It automatically runs in a background thread
questions.explain: Calling an async def function does not execute its body. It immediately returns a coroutine object, which only runs once it is awaited (or otherwise scheduled).

options: It runs a coroutine and pauses the enclosing coroutine until that coroutine completes, returning its result
It pauses the Python interpreter entirely for a fixed amount of time
It converts an async function into a regular function
It is purely decorative and has no effect on execution
questions.explain: await actually executes the coroutine it's given and suspends the current coroutine until a result comes back — this is the mechanism that lets other work happen during the wait.

options: Anywhere in a Python file, including the top level of a plain script
Only inside a for loop
Only inside a class definition
Only inside an async def function
questions.explain: await can only appear inside another async def (coroutine) function. Using it at the top level of an ordinary script is a SyntaxError — which is why coroutine code needs its own entry point like asyncio.run().

questions.q: A student calls `fetch_response("hello")` without await and is confused that nothing printed and the result looks like `<coroutine object ...>`. What's going on?
options: The function has a bug and needs to be rewritten
The function was called but not awaited, so its body never actually ran — only a coroutine object was created
Python silently ignored the function call
The print statement inside the function was deleted
questions.explain: This is the single most common beginner mistake with async/await: calling a coroutine function without awaiting it only creates a paused coroutine object. The body (and any print statements in it) never executes until it's awaited.

questions.q: Why can't `main()` in the lesson's example just be called directly like `main()` at the top of a script?
options: Because main is a reserved keyword in Python
Because coroutine functions can only be named main
Because main() is itself a coroutine function (defined with async def), so it must be run through something like asyncio.run(), not called directly
Because print() cannot be used inside async functions
questions.explain: Since main is defined with async def, calling main() alone would just produce another unawaited coroutine object. asyncio.run() is the entry point that actually starts the coroutine and runs it to completion — covered in the next lesson.
